question: Why is AC used in most large transport aircraft?

options.text: AC cannot cause an electric shock
AC needs no circuit protection at all
AC machines are simpler and lighter for their output
AC flows only in one direction, so it is easier to control

explanation: AC generators are simpler, more robust and have a better power-to-weight ratio than DC machines, among several other advantages.

question: Which is an advantage of AC over DC in aircraft?

options.text: AC motors need commutators for reliability
AC systems need heavier cables for the same power
AC cannot be converted into DC on board
Voltage can be changed efficiently with transformers

explanation: Transformers step AC voltage up or down at almost 100% efficiency, and TRUs give any DC voltage needed. Neither is possible so simply with DC.

question: How is DC obtained from an aircraft AC system?

options.text: Using a split ring commutator on each generator

explanation: Any required DC voltage is obtained simply and efficiently from AC with transformer rectifier units. Inverters do the opposite, DC to AC.

question: Why are AC machines more reliable at high altitude than DC machines?

options.text: They run hotter in the thin air

explanation: DC machines suffer commutator and brush problems that get worse at altitude; AC machines avoid commutation altogether.

question: How does cable weight of a high-voltage AC system compare with a low-voltage DC system of the same power?

options.text: It depends only on the cable insulation colour

explanation: Higher voltage means less current for the same power, so thinner, lighter cables can be used.

question: Which motors, run from a constant-frequency supply, are simpler and more efficient than DC motors?
explanation: Three-phase AC motors are simpler, more robust and more efficient than DC motors and run from a constant-frequency AC supply.

question: What is alternating current?

options.text: Current whose size changes but never reverses
Current produced only by a battery
Current flowing to and fro about a mean position
Current that flows steadily in one direction

explanation: In AC the electrons move back and forth about a mean position, reversing direction each half cycle.

question: What two things decide the size of the voltage from a simple AC generator?

options.text: Number of brushes and slip ring size
Speed of rotation and field strength
Battery voltage and frequency meter setting

explanation: Voltage depends on the rate of change of flux, which is set by the speed of rotation and the field strength.

question: Where in its rotation does a simple AC generator's loop induce no voltage?

options.text: Where its sides move at right angles to the field
Where its sides move parallel to the field
At every position, since output is constant

explanation: Moving parallel to the field there is no rate of change of flux and no voltage. Moving at right angles gives the maximum.

question: Why does the polarity of a simple AC generator's output reverse?

options.text: The field current reverses every half turn
The brushes swap slip rings every half turn
The battery reverses its polarity each cycle
Each side reverses direction through the field

explanation: As the loop passes through zero, each side starts moving the opposite way through the field, so the induced voltage and current reverse.

question: How can the instantaneous EMF of a rotating coil be calculated?

options.text: Maximum value × cosine of the frequency
Maximum value × sine of the phase angle
RMS value × the phase angle in degrees
Maximum value ÷ the number of poles

explanation: The induced EMF equals the peak value multiplied by the sine of the angle the coil has turned through, which traces a sine wave.

question: A sine wave voltage peaks at 200 V. What is its value 30° into the cycle?
explanation: e = Vmax × sin θ = 200 × sin 30° = 200 × 0.5 = 100 V. Using cosine gives 173 V, and the RMS value is 141 V.

question: What is a cycle?

options.text: The number of waveforms per second
The time for one complete waveform
One complete series of values of the waveform

explanation: A cycle is one complete set of values, from zero through positive and negative peaks back to the start.

question: How many degrees of phase does one cycle represent?
explanation: One cycle covers 0° to 360° of phase, matching one revolution of a two-pole generator.

question: What is frequency?

options.text: The angle between current and voltage
The maximum value in a cycle
The time taken for one cycle
The number of cycles per second

explanation: Frequency is cycles per second, measured in hertz. The time for one cycle is the period.

question: What is the usual frequency of a constant-frequency aircraft AC supply?
explanation: Constant-frequency aircraft AC systems usually run at 400 Hz. 50 and 60 Hz are domestic mains frequencies.

question: What does the frequency of an AC generator depend on?

options.text: The size of the load connected
How often N and S poles pass the armature
The thickness of the armature wire

explanation: Frequency depends on how many times a N and S pole pass the armature in a given time, so on the number of poles and the speed.

question: An 8-pole generator turns at 6000 RPM. What is its frequency?
explanation: f = (poles ÷ 2) × (RPM ÷ 60) = 4 × 100 = 400 Hz. Forgetting to halve the poles gives 800 Hz.

question: A 6-pole generator must produce 400 Hz. At what speed must it run?
explanation: RPM = f × 60 ÷ (poles ÷ 2) = 400 × 60 ÷ 3 = 8000 RPM. Using 6 instead of 3 gives 4000 RPM.

question: A 12-pole generator runs at 4000 RPM. What frequency does it produce?
In the frequency formula, what does "number of poles" mean?

options.text: The number of north poles only
The total of north and south poles
The number of pairs of brushes

explanation: It is the total number of N and S poles making up the field; it is then halved to give pole pairs.

question: What is the period of a waveform?

options.text: The time for half a cycle
The number of cycles per second
The peak value divided by frequency

explanation: Period T = 1 ÷ f seconds: the time taken for one complete cycle.

question: What is the period of a 400 Hz supply?
explanation: T = 1 ÷ 400 = 0.0025 s = 2.5 milliseconds.

question: What is the amplitude of a sine wave?

options.text: Its average value over a cycle
Its maximum (peak) value in a cycle

explanation: The amplitude or peak value is the maximum value the wave reaches in one cycle.

question: What is the RMS value of an alternating current?

options.text: The peak-to-peak value halved and squared
The average of the positive half cycle
The DC value that would produce the same heating
The highest value reached in the cycle

explanation: The RMS (effective) value is found by comparing AC with DC: it is the DC current giving the same heat in the same resistor.

question: Which makes a resistor hotter: 1 A DC, or AC with a 1 A peak?

options.text: It depends on the AC frequency

explanation: The AC is only at 1 A for an instant each half cycle; its effective value is 0.707 A, so the 1 A DC produces more heat.

question: How is the RMS value related to the peak value of a sine wave?
explanation: For a sine wave RMS = peak ÷ √2 = 0.707 × peak. 0.637 is the average value of a half cycle.

question: An aircraft AC supply is 115 V RMS. What is its peak voltage?
explanation: Peak = RMS × √2 = 115 × 1.414 ≈ 163 V. Multiplying by 0.707 gives 81 V, which is the wrong way round.

question: A sine wave has a peak value of 283 V. What is its RMS value?
explanation: RMS = 0.707 × 283 ≈ 200 V. 400 V would be multiplying by √2 instead.

question: How is the RMS value worked out from a waveform?

options.text: Add the peak values and divide by two
Multiply the frequency by the peak value
Average the instantaneous values over a half cycle
Square the values, average them, take the root

explanation: Root Mean Square: take instantaneous values, square them, find their mean, then take the square root.

question: In what values are aircraft AC supplies and meters usually stated?
explanation: Most AC supply values are given in RMS terms and ammeters and voltmeters are generally calibrated in RMS.

subtopic: Current and voltage in AC circuits
question: In an AC circuit, how do the current and voltage waveforms compare?

options.text: Current at twice the voltage frequency

explanation: Current and voltage have the same frequency and waveform shape, but may be out of phase depending on inductance and capacitance.

subtopic: Current and voltage in AC circuits
question: When are voltage and current said to be in phase?

options.text: They pass through zero and peak together

explanation: In phase means both pass through zero and reach their peaks in the same direction at the same moment, as in a resistive circuit.

subtopic: Current and voltage in AC circuits
question: What causes current and voltage to be out of phase?

options.text: The RMS value being lower than the peak
The frequency of the supply alone

explanation: The magnetic effect of inductance and the electrostatic effect of capacitance shift current relative to voltage.

subtopic: Current and voltage in AC circuits
question: What is phase angle?

options.text: The gap between matching points on the waves
The angle of the armature when the voltage is zero
The number of degrees in one cycle

explanation: Phase difference or phase angle is the angular gap between, for example, the voltage peak and the current peak.

question: Why is there no such thing as pure resistance in an AC circuit?

options.text: All conductors also have some inductance
AC cannot flow through a resistor

explanation: Even a straight wire has some inductance, though for study it is assumed circuits can be purely resistive, inductive or capacitive.

question: In a purely resistive AC circuit, current and voltage are:
explanation: With pure resistance both waveforms are in phase, and Ohm's law applies using RMS values.

question: How can a voltage be induced in a coil without any physical movement?

options.text: By varying the current in a nearby coil
By connecting it to a capacitor
By keeping a steady DC in a nearby coil

explanation: A changing current changes the magnetic field, and the changing field induces a voltage in a nearby coil with no motion.

question: A switch closes on a DC circuit with a coil beside a second coil and meter. What does the meter do?

options.text: Kicks once, then returns to zero
Shows a steady deflection while the switch is closed

explanation: The field expands only while the current is rising, inducing a brief pulse. Once the current is steady the field is static and nothing is induced.

question: The switch in that DC circuit is then opened. What does the meter do?

options.text: Kicks the opposite way, then zero
Kicks the same way as before

explanation: The collapsing field induces a pulse in the opposite direction to the one when the field was building up.

question: With AC in the primary coil, what does the meter in the secondary circuit show?

options.text: A current swinging both ways continuously
A single kick and then zero

explanation: The ever-changing AC field keeps inducing a voltage that alternates with the supply, so the meter swings back and forth.

question: When is the voltage induced by an AC current greatest?

options.text: At the 45° point of each cycle
When the current is at its peak

explanation: Induced voltage depends on the rate of change; a sine wave changes fastest as it passes through zero.

question: What is mutual induction the principle of?
explanation: A changing current in one coil inducing a voltage in another is mutual induction, the working principle of transformers.

question: The size of a mutually induced voltage depends on the rate of change of the field, which is proportional to:
explanation: The faster the field changes — the higher the frequency — the larger the induced voltage.

question: What is self-induction?

options.text: A capacitor discharging into its own plates
A coil inducing a voltage in itself
A coil inducing a voltage in a second coil
A generator exciting its own field from residual magnetism

explanation: A coil's own changing magnetic field induces a voltage in the coil itself.

question: By Lenz's law, the self-induced voltage in a coil:

options.text: Has no effect on the current
Doubles the current at every peak

explanation: The self-induced voltage, the back EMF, always opposes the change of current that produces it.

question: Which of these increases the inductance of a coil?
explanation: More turns and a soft iron core both strengthen the field and raise the coil's inductance.

question: What is the inductance of a coil a measure of?

options.text: Its ability to store electric charge
Its ability to produce a back EMF

explanation: Inductance is set by the coil's construction and measures its ability to produce a back EMF for a given rate of change of current.

question: What is the unit of inductance?
explanation: Inductance (symbol L) is measured in henries (H); practical values are often in millihenries or microhenries.

question: A circuit has an inductance of one henry when:

options.text: 1 A flows for 1 second through 1 ohm
A change of 1 A per second induces 1 V
A steady 1 A produces a 1 V drop

explanation: One henry is the inductance in which a current changing at one ampere per second induces a back EMF of one volt.

subtopic: Phase in inductive and capacitive circuits
question: In a purely inductive circuit, the current:

options.text: Is in phase with the voltage

explanation: Inductance holds back the rise of current behind the voltage; in a purely inductive circuit the lag is 90°.

subtopic: Phase in inductive and capacitive circuits
question: In a purely capacitive circuit, the current:

options.text: Is in phase with the voltage

explanation: The capacitor's charge and discharge make current lead voltage; in a purely capacitive circuit the lead is 90°.

subtopic: Phase in inductive and capacitive circuits
question: What does the mnemonic CIVIL describe?

options.text: C and L both make I lead V
In C, I leads V; in L, V leads I
C and L both keep I and V in phase
In C, V leads I; in L, I leads V

explanation: C-I-V: in a capacitive circuit current leads voltage. V-I-L: in an inductive circuit voltage leads current.

question: What is inductive reactance?

options.text: The charge stored by a coil
The resistance of the coil's wire to DC
The voltage induced in a second coil
The opposition to AC caused by inductance

explanation: Inductive reactance is the opposition inductance offers to alternating current; it depends on frequency as well as inductance.

question: What is the symbol and unit of inductive reactance?
explanation: Inductive reactance has the symbol XL and, like resistance, is measured in ohms.

question: What is the formula for inductive reactance?
explanation: XL = 2πfL, so it rises in direct proportion to frequency and inductance. 1/(2πfC) is the capacitive formula.

question: What is the reactance of a 10 mH coil at 400 Hz?
explanation: XL = 2π × 400 × 0.01 = 25.1 Ω. Using 10 instead of 0.01 H, or slipping a decimal place, gives the other figures.

question: How does increasing the frequency affect an inductive circuit?

options.text: XL falls and the current rises
XL rises and the current falls

explanation: XL is proportional to frequency, so higher frequency means more reactance and less current.

question: The supply frequency to an inductive circuit falls. What happens to the current?
explanation: Lower frequency reduces XL, so more current flows — which is why underfrequency can overload inductive equipment.

question: The frequency to a coil is doubled. Its inductive reactance:
explanation: XL = 2πfL is directly proportional to f, so doubling the frequency doubles the reactance.

question: What does a capacitor in a circuit resemble in a hydraulic system?

options.text: A pump driving fluid round the circuit
An accumulator storing fluid under pressure

explanation: Like an accumulator storing fluid under pressure, a capacitor stores an electrical charge once it has been charged.

question: Once charged and disconnected, how long does a practical capacitor hold its charge?

options.text: For ever, with no loss at all
Only while the supply frequency is maintained
A long time, slowly losing it by leakage
Only for a fraction of a second

explanation: In theory it would hold the charge indefinitely; in practice some leakage slowly discharges it.

question: How does a capacitor discharge compared with how it charged?
explanation: On discharge the current flows round the circuit in the opposite direction to the charging current; electrons never cross the dielectric.

question: A capacitor is one farad when:

options.text: 1 A for 1 s gives 1 V between its plates
1 V gives 1 A through its dielectric

explanation: One farad: a current of 1 A for 1 s (one coulomb) produces 1 V across the plates. Practical capacitors are in microfarads or picofarads.

question: What is the symbol and unit of capacitive reactance?
explanation: Capacitive reactance has the symbol XC and is measured in ohms.

question: What is the formula for capacitive reactance?
explanation: XC = 1/(2πfC): it is inversely proportional to frequency and capacitance.

question: What is the reactance of a 10 µF capacitor at 400 Hz?
explanation: XC = 1/(2π × 400 × 10 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/0.0251 ≈ 39.8 Ω. Forgetting the reciprocal gives 0.025.

question: How does increasing frequency affect a capacitive circuit?

options.text: XC rises and the current falls
XC falls and the current rises

explanation: XC is inversely proportional to frequency, so higher frequency means less reactance and more current.

question: The frequency to a capacitor is halved. Its capacitive reactance:
explanation: XC = 1/(2πfC); halving f doubles XC.

question: What is impedance?

options.text: The power lost as heat in a circuit
The total opposition to AC, in ohms
The reactance of a capacitor only
The resistance of a circuit to DC only

explanation: Impedance (Z) combines resistance and the net reactance and is the total opposition to alternating current, measured in ohms.

question: Why can't resistance and reactance simply be added to find impedance?

options.text: They are 90° out of phase with each other
Reactance is always zero at 400 Hz
They are measured in different units

explanation: Resistance and reactance act 90° apart, so they must be added as vectors (Pythagoras), not arithmetically.

question: How are inductive and capacitive reactance combined?

options.text: By subtracting one from the other

explanation: XL and XC are 180° apart (current lags in one, leads in the other), so the net reactance is their difference.

question: A circuit has R = 6 Ω, XL = 10 Ω and XC = 2 Ω. What is its impedance?
explanation: Net X = 10 − 2 = 8 Ω; Z = √(6² + 8²) = 10 Ω. Adding everything gives 18 Ω, and 8 Ω is the reactance alone.

question: What is the symbol for impedance?
explanation: Impedance is given the symbol Z; reactance is X, resistance R and inductance L.

question: When is a circuit resonant?
explanation: Because XL rises and XC falls with frequency, there is one frequency at which they are equal: the resonant frequency.

question: In a series circuit of inductance and capacitance, the current at resonance is:
explanation: At resonance in series the reactances cancel, leaving only resistance, so the current is maximum.

question: In a parallel circuit of inductance and capacitance, the current at resonance is:
explanation: At resonance in parallel the circuit offers maximum opposition, so the supply current is minimum.

question: Raising the supply frequency has what effect on XL and XC?
explanation: XL = 2πfL rises with frequency; XC = 1/(2πfC) falls with it. This opposite behaviour is what allows resonance.

question: Why is actual power in a reactive AC circuit not always V × I?

options.text: Voltage and current are out of phase

explanation: When current and voltage are out of phase, the power actually absorbed is less than the apparent product of volts and amps.

question: In a purely resistive circuit, the power curve is:

options.text: At the same frequency as the supply
Always positive, at twice the supply frequency

explanation: With V and I in phase their product is always positive, and the power wave has twice the supply frequency.

question: In a purely resistive circuit, the true power equals:
explanation: True (real, wattful) power in a resistive circuit is the product of RMS voltage and RMS current, in watts.

question: What is true power also called?
explanation: True power is also called real, effective, wattful or working power, measured in watts or kW.

question: In a purely inductive circuit, what is the true power?
explanation: Power given to build the magnetic field is returned as it collapses, so positive and negative power are equal and no real power is absorbed.

question: What is reactive power measured in?
explanation: Reactive power — volt-amps reactive — is measured in VAR or kVAR.

question: What is apparent power?

options.text: The power returned to the supply, in VAR
RMS volts × RMS amps, in VA or kVA
The heat lost in the cables, in watts
RMS volts × RMS amps × power factor, in watts

explanation: Apparent power is the simple product of RMS voltage and current, measured in VA or kVA, also called theoretical or rated power.

question: In a purely capacitive circuit, how much real power is absorbed?

options.text: Only the power needed to heat the plates

explanation: As with pure inductance, positive and negative power are equal, so the true power is zero and all power is reactive.

question: In a practical circuit with resistance and inductance, the true power is:

options.text: The peak of the power curve
The average of the power curve
The negative part of the power curve

explanation: With both R and L, positive power exceeds negative power, and the average of the power curve is the true power consumed.

question: A circuit has equal resistance and inductive reactance. What is the phase angle?
explanation: With R = XL the impedance triangle is isosceles, so the phase angle is 45° with current lagging.

question: What is power factor?
explanation: Power factor = true power (kW) ÷ apparent power (kVA). It can also be found as the cosine of the phase angle.

question: Power factor can also be calculated as:

options.text: The tangent of the phase angle
The sine of the phase angle
The cosine of the phase angle

explanation: PF = cos φ. cos 0° = 1 (resistive), cos 90° = 0 (purely reactive).

question: What is the power factor of a purely resistive circuit?
explanation: Phase angle is 0°, true power equals apparent power, and cos 0° = 1 — the maximum.

question: What is the power factor of a purely inductive circuit?
explanation: Phase angle 90°, true power zero, cos 90° = 0 — the minimum.

question: As the phase angle in a circuit decreases, the power factor:
explanation: A smaller phase angle brings true power closer to apparent power, so the power factor rises towards 1.

question: A load draws 40 kVA and consumes 32 kW. What is its power factor?
explanation: PF = 32 ÷ 40 = 0.8. Dividing the other way gives 1.25, which is impossible for a power factor.

question: A 115 V load draws 10 A at a power factor of 0.8. What true power does it use?
explanation: True power = V × I × PF = 115 × 10 × 0.8 = 920 W. 1150 W is the apparent power (VA) and 1437 W divides by the PF instead.

question: A load has an apparent power of 50 kVA and a true power of 40 kW. What is its reactive power?
explanation: The power triangle gives kVAR = √(50² − 40²) = √900 = 30. Subtracting directly gives 10, which ignores the 90° relationship.

question: A circuit has a phase angle of 60°. What is its power factor?
When does true power equal apparent power?

options.text: When the circuit is purely inductive
When the frequency is exactly 400 Hz
When voltage and current are in phase
When they are 90° out of phase

explanation: True power equals apparent power only in phase (power factor 1). At 90° out of phase true power is zero.
